overview: F2101 introduces the formation mindset before the airplane work becomes dense: Lead must provide a predictable platform, Wing must preserve sight and spacing, and both aircraft must use disciplined communications and small position corrections during departure, recovery, and basic formation maneuvering.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Formation departures and arrivals are built around predictable Lead actions, runway-side discipline, and enough spacing for Wing to correct without rushing.

children.text: Lead normally lines up on the downwind side so wake turbulence and prop wash move away from Wing.
Both aircraft complete the Lineup Checklist while crossing the hold-short line and center themselves on their assigned runway side.
Wing confirms Lead's runway side, then taxis forward until Wing's leading edge aligns with Lead's horizontal stabilizer trailing edge.
The runway must be at least 100 ft wide for an interval takeoff.
Lead passes the run-up signal; both aircraft set about 30% torque and check safety-of-flight items and engine instruments.
Wing visually inspects Lead and holds the thumbs-up until Lead acknowledges.
Lead gives the kiss-off and begins a maximum-power takeoff on the assigned side; Wing starts the takeoff roll 5 seconds later, creating about 1000 ft of spacing.
After takeoff, Lead flies the briefed departure and gives Wing a stable, predictable rejoin platform.
Local formation guidance uses about 80% torque and 160 KIAS until Wing joins; if a turn is required before join, keep the bank shallow enough for Wing to close safely.
Wing keeps Lead slightly above the horizon, manages closure, and moves inside a departure turn when that helps the rendezvous.
During a running rendezvous, keep closure controlled; the local event source limits closure to no more than 40 KIAS until joined.
Lead normally directs Wing to cruise for checks and weather, then brings Wing back to parade before entering tower or pattern airspace.
Use only the current SOP, course rules, and day-of brief for local routing, frequencies, and field-specific reporting points.
During recovery descents, Lead should remain stable and normally keep at least 15% torque; Wing may need idle power and speed brake to maintain position.
For the break or section approach, Lead plans the spacing problem early and gives Wing clear detach, break, or speed-brake direction.

items.text: Formation is a shared task, but responsibilities are different: Lead owns the platform and plan; Wing owns sight, position, and deconfliction.

children.text: The Designated Flight Lead is the administrative lead assigned for mission objectives and safe, orderly conduct.
The Formation Lead is the aircraft physically flying lead at that moment.
Formation Lead must make smooth, stable, predictable changes in power, heading, and altitude.
Lead keeps the flight in the assigned area, clear of clouds unless on an IFR clearance, and clear of other aircraft.
Lead must always know where Wing is and must execute the briefed sequence with proper visual or radio communications.
Keep Lead in sight and maintain flight-path deconfliction.
Maintain proper formation position and make small, timely corrections.
Comply with Lead's signals and give timely responses.
Provide mutual support by backing up navigation, communications, fuel awareness, and safety-of-flight decisions.
Everything takes longer in formation, especially frequency changes, checklist work, turns, and rejoins.
Lead must plan ahead for area boundaries, wind drift, sun angle, Wing workload, and how each maneuver sets up the next one.

items.text: Clear communications prevent confusion before it becomes a spacing problem.

children.text: Use the ATC call sign with outside agencies and the tactical call sign for inter-flight communication.
Brief primary and secondary UHF and VHF tactical frequencies before flight.
Lead handles outside-agency communications; Wing monitors and backs up Lead.
Wing is responsible for staying on the correct frequency and querying Lead if unsure.
Do not conduct formation check-ins on ATC frequencies unless directed; use tactical frequency to get well.
Lead must give Wing enough time to change frequencies before transmitting to the controlling agency.
Use positive check-ins after directed switches so both aircraft know the flight is together.
Use visual signals when they are clear and briefed.
Use radio calls in IMC, when there is confusion, or whenever a visual signal may be missed.
Lead should provide a stable platform during any radio or visual communication task.

items.text: Position corrections start with relative motion: Lead is the reference, and Wing fixes altitude, bearing, then closure in that order.

children.text: Altitude is the first correction because step-down protects separation.
Bearing line is second; acute means forward of the bearing line, sucked means aft of it.
Closure or separation is last; do not close distance until altitude and bearing are under control.
Vertical movement is primarily controlled with elevator.
Fore and aft movement is controlled with power.
Left and right movement is controlled with aileron.
Every correction needs a re-correction: add the input, stop the movement, then reset a middle value.
When Lead turns into Wing, Wing is on a smaller radius and must reduce power early or become acute.
When Lead turns away from Wing, Wing is on a larger radius and must add power early or become sucked.
Lead every turn with the required power change, then scan the whole aircraft instead of fixating on one checkpoint.

studyNotes.summary: F2101 is the first formation simulator event, so the study focus is the basic contract: predictable Lead, disciplined Wing, clear communications, and small A-B-C position corrections.

summary: F2101 introduces formation departure, arrival, communication, responsibility, and position-correction fundamentals for the first linked formation simulator event.
title: Formation Arrival and Departure Procedures
